talk: LTV to CAC compares what a customer is worth over their whole time with you to what it cost to win them. A ratio of 3 to 1 is a common healthy target. Much lower and you're overpaying for customers, much higher and you may be spending too little on growth.

terms.meaning: Lifetime value. Total profit from one customer over all the years they stay.
Customer acquisition cost. What you spend to win one new customer.
LTV divided by CAC. How many dollars come back for each dollar spent winning a customer.

questions.prompt: A club membership makes $120 profit a year and the average member stays 3 years. It costs $90 to win a member. What's the LTV to CAC ratio?
questions.hint: Lifetime value first, then divide by the cost to win.
whyNot: $120 / $90 = about 1.3 uses one year of profit. Members stay 3 years, so count all three.
3 to 1 is the usual target, not your number. Yours is $360 / $90 = 4.
40 to 1 is too big by 10 times. $360 / $90 = 4.

questions.prompt: You want a ratio of at least 3 to 1. With an LTV of $360, what's the most you should spend to win a member?
questions.hint: LTV divided by the target ratio.
whyNot: $90 is what you spend now. You could spend up to $120 and still hit 3 to 1.
$360 / 2 = $180 gives a ratio of 2 to 1. That's below your target.
$360 is the whole lifetime value. Spend that and you'd make nothing.

questions.prompt: A new referral scheme wins members for $40 each, but referred members only stay 2 years. They still make $120 a year. What's their LTV to CAC ratio?
questions.hint: New lifetime value, new cost to win.
working: They stay for less time, but they're so cheap to win that the ratio is better. Spend more on referrals.
whyNot: $120 / $40 = 3 uses one year of profit. Referred members stay 2 years.
4 to 1 is the ratio for ordinary members. Referred members are a different deal.
$360 / $40 = 9 uses the old 3-year LTV. Referred members only stay 2 years.

penalty.prompt: A member makes {profit} profit a year and stays {years} years. Winning a member costs {cac}. What's the LTV to CAC ratio? (Type the first number, like 3 for 3 to 1.)
penalty.hint: Lifetime value first, then divide by the cost to win.
working: {profit * years|usd} / {cac} = {profit * years / cac|num}, so {profit * years / cac|num} to 1.

traps.why: That uses one year of profit. Members stay {years} years.
Upside down. Divide the lifetime value by the cost to win.

call.title: The agency pitch
call.prompt: A marketing agency offers 1,000 new fans for $400,000, which is $400 each, but they come from a one-off ticket giveaway. Your referral scheme brings 300 fans at $50 each, and referred fans tend to stay. Over 20 matchdays a fan who stays is worth 20 x $18 = $360.

options.label: Sign the agency
options.result: $360 / $400 = 0.9, so 0.9 to 1 even if they stayed, and they don't. Cheap-looking growth that churns is the most expensive kind.

later.text: The agency's fans were one-match tourists. Almost none come back.

options.label: Run the referral scheme
options.result: Good call. 300 x $50 = $15,000, and $360 / $50 = 7.2, so 7.2 to 1. Cheap fans worth far more than they cost.

options.label: Do both
options.result: The referral fans are a great deal, but the agency half loses money. Don't let a good deal hide a bad one.

later.text: The agency's fans drift away. The referral fans stay.

takeaway: Spend to win customers while each dollar brings back about three. Watch both numbers, not just one.
